query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post‐deposition thermal treatment of the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating in an oxidizing environment induces the in situ formation of a continuous chromium‐rich oxide scale (primarily Cr2O3 with accompanying spinel phases) that enhances overall wear resistance at high temperatures by both increasing the surface hardness and providing a lubricious barrier that reduces friction and abrasive damage.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate (e.g., SS-304) with a fine, homogeneous microstructure and evenly distributed alloying elements.
generation.intervention: Apply a post-deposition thermal treatment at approximately 800 °C in air for an optimized duration to enable controlled oxidation of the surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear conditions (around 800 °C) under sliding contact with a moderate load (e.g., ~15 N) and typical sliding speeds encountered in the intended application.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent, nanoscale Cr2O3-rich oxide layer along with minor spinel phases (such as (Fe,Co,Ni,Cr,Cu)3O4) on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the controlled oxidation—catalyzed by the presence of chromium—leads to growth of a dense oxide film. This oxide protects the underlying alloy by both serving as a physical barrier that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and as a solid lubricant that decreases shear strength at the interface, thereby lowering friction and mitigating wear. The oxide’s formation also slightly increases surface hardness which further supports wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline coating, the thermally treated coating will exhibit a significantly reduced wear rate and lower coefficient of friction during high-temperature sliding tests, attributed to the protective oxide film.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating without any additional thermal treatment, which lacks the optimized continuous oxide scale.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature conditions (approximately 800 °C) and sliding wear under moderate loads (around 15 N). At lower temperatures or drastically different sliding conditions, the oxide-mediated protection may not form or be effective.
generation.uncertainty: While previous studies (e.g., PMC10908794 evidence on HEA coatings forming protective Cr2O3 layers) support the beneficial role of controlled oxidation, there is uncertainty about the detailed oxide phase stability and adherence dynamics in FeNiCrCoCu compared to other similar HEA systems. The influence of the specific Cr content and its interactions with the other elements under dynamic wear conditions remains to be fully validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on a metal substrate: one set as-deposited and one set subjected to the proposed thermal treatment (≈800 °C in air for a specified duration). Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests under identical conditions (e.g., 800 °C, 15 N load, defined sliding speed and distance) for both sets.
measurements: Surface oxide composition and continuity (using SEM, EDS, and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the thermally treated coatings do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., reduced wear rate and lower friction coefficient) compared to the as-deposited baseline, or if surface analysis reveals a discontinuous or non-adherent oxide layer.
